question: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The EU acts as the custodian of Europe’s agricultural biodiversity heritage – one of the most important in the world, built over centuries through the work of millions of farmers who have handpicked, conserved and promoted native varieties closely connected with the local area. Products bearing the PDO, PGI, DOC and DOCG labels form a pillar of Europe’s agri-food economy. Small and medium-sized farms and family businesses play a key role in protecting the rural landscape, conserving biodiversity and looking after inland areas. The revision of the EU’s rules on new genomic techniques (NGT)1 unlocks major opportunities for the farming sector to innovate, but also raises questions as regards the impact on biodiversity, farmers’ freedom of choice, product traceability and the increasingly concentrated seed market. In light of the above: 1.

What steps will the Commission take to ensure that the future NGT rules do not endanger Europe’s agricultural biodiversity or undermine the conservation of native varieties and the protection of certified PDO, PGI, DOC and DOCG products?
In the interests of transparency, freedom of choice for consumers and safeguards for farmers, how will it ensure effective traceability mechanisms for NGT products?
What initiatives will it promote to strike the right balance between scientific innovation, protecting Europe’s genetic heritage and the economic viability of farms?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260611IPR45215/new-genomic-techniques-forplants-to-boost-innovation-in-sustainable-agriculture 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) Regulation (EU) 2026/13881, adopted on 17 June 2026 by the European Parliament and the Council, creates an enabling regulatory framework for plants obtained by New Genomic Techniques (NGT) so that breeders can diversify plant reproductive material to find solutions for pressing challenges that farmers face today, such as crops more resilient to climate change or requiring less fertilisers and pesticides. As set out in the Regulation, the Commission will monitor the impacts of NGT plants, including as regards the issues raised by the Honourable Member. The Regulation distinguishes two situations on traceability. Category 1 NGT plants, considered equivalent to conventional plants and their products, do not require traceability or specific labelling. Transparency is ensured through seed labelling, a public register of NGT plants, and information in plant variety catalogues. Category 2 NGT plants and products, featuring more complex modifications, remain subject to the traceability and labelling of the Genetically modified organisms regulatory framework. The Commission will support the proper implementation of these new rules as set out in its implementation strategy2. Geographical Indications, through their legal specifications, help producers obtain fair value for their products and support rural employment, thereby safeguarding the economic viability of farmers. They also preserve traditions, while allowing producers to innovate, provided the product keeps its essential link to its origin and recognised characteristics. Various EU-funded projects are advancing innovation in agriculture, including in the area of NGTs while addressing technical, socio-economic and other dimensions.
1 New Genomic Techniques (NGT) Regulation - Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of

the Council of 17 June 2026 on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products, and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (OJ L, 2026/1388, 26.6.2026, ELI: https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1388). 2 https://food.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4c13763b-bed7-40f1-800956fc4b7c7a57_en?filename=ngt_leg_implementation-strategy_reg-2026-1388.pdf.
